source_text: Καὶ ὅπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ Στεφάνου γέγονε, τοῦτο καὶ ἐπ' ἐκείνου συνέβαινεν. Ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐκ ἰσχύοντες ἀντιστῆναι τῇ σοφίᾳ τῇ τοῦ Στεφάνου, οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι ἐλίθαζον τὸν ἅγιον ἐκεῖνον· οὕτω καὶ οὗτοι οὐκ ἰσχύοντες ἀντιστῆναι τῇ σοφίᾳ τῇ τούτου, καὶ ὁρῶντες ἠσφαλισμένα τὰ ὀχυρώματα, ἐκβάλλουσι τῆς πόλεως λοιπὸν τὸν κήρυκα. Ἀλλ' ἡ φωνὴ οὐκ ἐσίγα, ἀλλ' ἐξεβάλλετο μὲν ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὁ δὲ λόγος τῆς διδασκαλίας οὐκ ἐξεβάλλετο. Καὶ γὰρ Παῦλος ἐδέδετο, καὶ ὁ λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐκ ἐδέδετο· καὶ οὗτος ἐν ἀλλοτρίᾳ, καὶ ἡ διδασκαλία αὐτοῦ παρ' ἡμῖν. Ἐκ βάλλοντες τοίνυν ἐπεισῄεσαν συμφραξάμενοι, καθά περ χείμαῤῥος σφοδρός· ἀλλ' οὔτε τὰ φυτὰ παρέσυραν, οὔτε τὰ σπέρματα κατέχωσαν, οὔτε τὴν γεωργίαν ἐλυμήναντο· οὕτω καλῶς καὶ μετ' ἐπιστήμης ὑπὸ τῆς ἐκείνου γεωργηθέντα σοφίας ἐῤῥίζωτο. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἄξιον εἰπεῖν, τίνος ἕνεκεν συνεχώρησεν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεὸς ἀπελαθῆναι ἐντεῦθεν. Προσφάτως ἦν ἀναπνεύσασα ἡ Ἐκκλησία· εἶχε παραμυθίαν οὐ τὴν τυχοῦσαν τὴν ἐπιστασίαν τὴν ἐκείνου· πανταχόθεν αὐτὴν ἐτείχιζεν, καὶ τῶν πολεμίων τὰς προσβολὰς ἀπεκρούετο. Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν ἐξεβάλλετο, καὶ συνεχώρει τοῖς ἀπάγουσιν αὐτὸν ὁ Θεός; τίνος ἕνεκεν; Καὶ μή τοι νομίσητε ταύτης τῆς ἀπορίας λύσιν εἶναι τὸ λεγόμενον μόνης· ἀλλὰ κἂν πρὸς Ἕλληνας, κἂν πρὸς αἱρε τικοὺς ἄλλους ὑμῖν ὑπὲρ τῶν τοιούτων γίνηται λόγος, ἱκανὸν τὸ ῥηθησόμενον ἅπασαν λῦσαι τὴν ἀπορίαν. Ὁ Θεὸς τὴν μὲν πίστιν αὐτοῦ τὴν ἀληθῆ καὶ ἀποστο λικὴν ἐν πολλοῖς συγχωρεῖ πολεμεῖσθαι, τὰς δὲ αἱρέ σεις καὶ τὸν ἑλληνισμὸν ἀφίησιν ἀδείας ἀπο λαύειν. Τί δήποτε; Ἵνα ἐκείνων μὲν τὴν ἀσθένειαν μάθῃς οὐκ ἐνοχλουμένων, καὶ αὐτομάτως καταλυο μένων· τῆς δὲ πίστεως τὴν ἰσχὺν γνωρίσῃς πολεμου μένης, καὶ διὰ τῶν κωλυόντων αὐξανομένης. Καὶ ὅτι οὐκ ἐμός ἐστιν οὗτος στοχασμὸς, ἀλλὰ θεῖος χρησμὸς ἄνωθεν ἐνεχθεὶς, ἀκούσωμεν Παύλου τί περὶ τούτων φησί· καὶ γὰρ ἔπαθέ τί ποτε ἀνθρώπινον καὶ οὗτος· εἰ γὰρ καὶ Παῦλος ἦν, ἀλλὰ τῆς ἡμετέρας μετέσχε φύσεως. Τί δέ ἐστιν, ὅπερ ἔπαθεν; Ἠλαύνετο, ἐπολεμεῖτο, ἐμαστίζετο, μυρίοις ἐπεβουλεύετο τρόποις, ἔξωθεν, ἔσωθεν, ὑπὸ τῶν δοκούντων οἰκείων εἶναι, ὑπὸ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων. Καὶ τί δεῖ λέγειν, ὅσας ὑπέμεινε θλίψεις; Κάμνων τοίνυν, καὶ μηκέτι φέρων τὰς προσ βολὰς τῶν πολεμίων ἀεὶ διακοπτόντων αὐτοῦ τὴν δι δασκαλίαν, καὶ ἐναντιουμένων αὐτοῦ τῷ λόγῳ, προσ πίπτει τῷ Δεσπότῃ, καὶ παρακαλεῖ αὐτὸν, καὶ λέγει· Ἐδόθη μοι σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκὶ ἄγγελος Σατᾶν, ἵνα με κολαφίζῃ· ὑπὲρ τούτου τρὶς τὸν Κύριον παρεκάλεσα, καὶ εἴρηκέ μοι· Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου· ἡ γὰρ δύναμίς μου ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελειοῦται. Καὶ οἶδα μὲν ὅτι τινὲς ἀσθένειαν εἶναι νομίζουσι σωμα τικήν· οὐκ ἔστι δὲ τοῦτο, οὐκ ἔστιν· ἀλλ' ἄγγελον Σατᾶν τοὺς ἀντικειμένους ἀνθρώπους καλεῖ· τὸ γὰρ Σατᾶν τοῦτο Ἑβραϊκὴ λέξις ἐστί· Σατᾶν δὲ ὁ ἀντικείμενος λέγεται. Τὰ οὖν σκεύη τοῦ διαβόλου, καὶ τοὺς ἐκείνῳ διακονουμένους ἀνθρώπους ἀγγέλους αὐ τοῦ καλεῖ. Διὰ τί οὖν, φησὶ, πρόσκειται τῇ σαρκί; Ὅτι ἡ σὰρξ ἐμαστίζετο, ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ ἐκουφίζετο τῇ ἐλπίδι τῶν μελλόντων ἐπαιρομένη· οὐδὲ γὰρ ἥπτετο τῆς ψυχῆς, οὐδὲ ὑπεσκέλιζε τοὺς ἔνδον λογισμοὺς, ἀλλὰ μέχρι τῆς σαρκὸς εἱστήκει τὰ μηχανήματα καὶ ὁ πόλεμος, εἴσω διαβῆναι μὴ δυνάμενος.
thought_title: Why God permits the faithful to be attacked
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why God allowed Eustathius to be expelled from Antioch, and he turns to Paul's experience of the thorn in the flesh to show that God permits attacks on true faith to reveal its strength.
pass_a_gloss: And what happened in the case of Stephen, this also happened in the case of that man. For just as the Jews, not being strong enough to withstand the wisdom of Stephen, were stoning that holy man, so also these men, not being strong enough to withstand the wisdom of this man, and seeing the strongholds made secure, cast out the herald from the city from then on. But the voice was not silent, but the man was being cast out, but the word of teaching was not cast out. For indeed Paul was bound, and the word of God was not bound; and this man was in a foreign land, and his teaching was among us. Casting him out then they came in having banded together, just like a violent torrent; but they neither swept away the plants, nor buried the seeds, nor harmed the cultivation; so well and with skill had the things cultivated by that man's wisdom been rooted. But indeed it is worth saying for what reason God permitted him to be driven away from here. The church had recently recovered its breath; it had no ordinary consolation in his oversight; from every side he was walling it around, and he was beating back the attacks of the enemies. For what reason then was he being cast out, and God was permitting those who were leading him away? For what reason? And do not suppose that the thing said is a solution of this difficulty only; but even if against Greeks, even if against other heretics a discussion arises among you about such matters, the thing about to be said is sufficient to solve the whole difficulty. God permits his true and apostolic faith to be warred against in many ways, but he allows the heresies and paganism to enjoy freedom from fear. Why ever? In order that you may learn the weakness of those things when they are not troubled, and when they are destroyed of their own accord; and that you may recognize the strength of the faith when it is warred against, and when it grows through those who hinder it. And that this is not my conjecture, but a divine oracle brought from above, let us hear Paul what he says about these things; for he also suffered something human at some time, this man too; for even if he was Paul, nevertheless he shared in our nature. And what is it that he suffered? He was being driven out, he was being warred against, he was being scourged, he was being plotted against in countless ways, from outside, from inside, by those who seemed to be of his own household, by strangers. And why is it necessary to say how many afflictions he endured? Being weary then, and no longer bearing the attacks of the enemies who were always cutting through his teaching, and opposing his word, he falls before the Master, and entreats him, and says: There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, in order that he might buffet me; about this I entreated the Lord three times, and he has said to me: My grace is sufficient for you; for my power is made perfect in weakness. And I know that some think that it is a bodily weakness; but this is not so, it is not; but he calls the opposing human beings a messenger of Satan; for this Satan is a Hebrew word; and Satan means the one who opposes. The vessels of the devil then, and the human beings who serve him, he calls his messengers. Why then, he says, is it attached to the flesh? Because the flesh was being scourged, but the soul was being lightened, being lifted up by the hope of things to come; for it did not touch the soul, nor did it trip up the inner thoughts, but the devices and the war stood still up to the flesh, not being able to pass inside.

choices.why: Glossary term; Chrysostom explicitly interprets this as human opponents serving Satan, so the literal rendering preserves his exegesis.
Glossary term; the literal rendering keeps the bodily locus that Chrysostom contrasts with the soul.
Glossary term; refers to the catholic church, here the church of Antioch recovering from persecution.
Glossary term; the Arian heresy and others are meant, not merely sects.
Glossary term; the earlier external enemy contrasted with internal heresy.
In Paul's quotation, weakness is the literal sense and Chrysostom argues against reading it as bodily illness; the literal rendering preserves the ambiguity he addresses.

pass_b_english: And what happened in Stephen’s case happened in his as well. Just as the Jews, unable to withstand Stephen’s wisdom, were stoning that holy man, so these men, unable to withstand his wisdom and seeing the strongholds secured, finally cast the herald out of the city. But the voice did not fall silent: the man was cast out, but the word of his teaching was not cast out. Paul was in chains, and the word of God was not in chains (2 Timothy 2:9); so too this man was in a foreign land, and his teaching remained among us. So they banded together and swept in like a violent torrent—but they neither swept away the plants nor buried the seeds nor harmed the cultivation, so well and skillfully had they been rooted by his wisdom. But it is worth saying why God permitted him to be driven away from here. The church had recently recovered its breath; his oversight was no small comfort to it. He was walling it around on every side and beating back the assaults of its enemies. Why then was he cast out, and why did God permit those who were taking him away? Why? Do not think that what I am about to say resolves only this difficulty; even if you are debating with pagans or with other heretics about such matters, what will be said is enough to resolve the whole difficulty. God allows his true and apostolic faith to be fought against in many ways, but he lets the heresies and paganism enjoy freedom from disturbance. Why is that? So that you may learn the weakness of the latter from the fact that they collapse on their own even when no one troubles them, and so that you may recognize the strength of the faith from the fact that it is fought against and yet grows through those who try to hinder it. And to show that this is not my own conjecture but a divine oracle sent from above, let us hear what Paul says about these things—for he too once suffered something human. Even if he was Paul, he still shared our nature. What was it he suffered? He was driven out, fought against, scourged, plotted against in countless ways—from outside, from inside, by those who seemed to be his own and by strangers. Why need I say how many afflictions he endured? So, growing weary and no longer bearing the assaults of enemies who were constantly cutting short his teaching and opposing his word, he falls before the Master and pleads with him, saying: “A thorn in the flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan, to strike me. Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). I know that some think this weakness is bodily—but it is not, it is not. He calls the opposing human beings a messenger of Satan. For “Satan” is a Hebrew word, and “Satan” means “the one who opposes.” So he calls the instruments of the devil, the human beings who serve him, his messengers. Why then, he says, is it attached to the flesh? Because the flesh was being scourged, while the soul was being lifted up, raised high by hope in the things to come. For it did not touch the soul, nor did it trip up the reasoning within; the devices and the war stopped at the flesh, unable to pass inside.
